name: Happiness as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue
plain_explanation: For Aristotle, being happy is not a passive feeling but a matter of actively living and acting well, exercising your best capacities, over a complete life.
precise_definition: Aristotle's central ethical claim that 'the good' is happiness (eudaimonia), and that happiness consists in 'activity of soul in accordance with virtue in a complete life,' with the rational soul's contemplative activity representing its highest and most complete form.
why_it_mattered: It makes Aristotle's ethics teleological (aimed at a final good) rather than rule-based, and ties ethical theory directly to his metaphysical account of the soul and its rational and irrational parts.
historical_origin: Set out at the start of the Nicomachean Ethics.
examples: The claim that a man cannot be called happy 'on the rack,' since some degree of external good fortune is necessary for happiness
competing_positions: Those who regard pleasure itself, rather than virtuous activity, as the good, and so treat virtue purely as a means
influence_on_later_thinkers: Provides the ethical foundation for the later doctrines of the golden mean and of contemplation as the highest happiness.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Because Aristotle considers ethics a branch of politics, this definition of happiness underlies his views on the best form of government.
